utterances.text: All right. Did you know that Mr. Valenta had never held any office in the political party, the HDZ BiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As he was a member in the hierarchy, he had some political duties, because usually people in executive boards of parties had political duties. That was their main role.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This gentleman, Mr. Valenta, is currently a member of the committee on borders of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, isn't he? Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that from the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But he's still an expert on certain matters who actually works for the present government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that he was an expert, but he's at the head of an expert team, and those team members prepare the specialised material on the basis of which the lines were drawn between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. All that I have been able to see in the press of both Croatia and Bosnia shows that the institute in Split was involved, also institutions in Zagreb, some institutes in Zagreb. So in my view, that agreement was based on concrete data, and I would be free to say that those borders were fixed without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't mean to interrupt you, but you're sort of straying from the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just for the Trial Chamber's information, I have about five minutes of questions on this particular book, about two minutes of questions on the final subject, and I should be through before 20 to 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I might show you the book that's already in evidence, at least my -- I've highlighted certain portions of it to facilitate quick travel through here; I think it's Z9. And I might point out, I don't know whether the part of this book that -- whether the version of this book that's been entered into evidence is complete or not. The version that we have is actually incomplete; it lacks the final pages and appendices. If we could just turn to the first item that I've tabbed, sir, and I've highlighted it in yellow, you would agree that Mr. Valenta --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I have page references so that I can follow, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. In the version we have, there is no actual page number, but there is an ERN number, and it is 00257120.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The book is dedicated as follows, is it not, sir: "I dedicate this book to my sons and my --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This is a quote from this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the dedication finishes with the hope that they will never experience war in this region. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you certainly agree --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is it. That is on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, and you agreed with that when you read the book, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The point is, you agree with that sentiment, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is like a motto of a book, and from the human state, point, this is a very nice motto to have put on the cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to turn to page 4 in the Croatian version, the next page that I have highlighted. In his introductory comments, Mr. Valenta makes this point: "I am not insisting on any of the concepts. Most of them are just options for the regional partition of BH within the existing borders. The reader will draw his own conclusion." Mr. Valenta did not insist upon any of the ideas in this book; it was merely a description of certain options that were open to the emerging Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina before the actual referendum was held in the end of February and early March, 1992. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my statement, I said that in reading the book, this was unusual, because it took a standpoint which was never done before with respect to the population in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and from that point of view, it was a surprise. And I also now recall that throughout the book, that is how it was put, that these were ideas that could be seen throughout the book, that it could be this way, it could be that way. But what I said was that the ideas have been followed to its consequences from the book, which ended up in ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: At the time that this book was written, it's true that the SDS political party representing the Bosnian Serbs, and the Bosnian Serb people themselves, had actually virtually unanimously refused to endorse the concept of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in fact --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And they also did not recognise the independence of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it's true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers, regarding this point, I should like the witness to be asked to clarify what he said on two occasions, I think, in his examination-in-chief and now in the cross-examination, that when he read this book, he found that it was unusual; he was surprised that it addressed these problems in this way. Does that mean, Witness N, that for you, the various ethnicities or people of different ethnic background are naturally called to live together rather than to be separated? Is that how you saw things before reading this book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The way I used to view these issues before having read the book are the same as I still hold now. But what I can say is, with respect to Central Bosnia, Bosniaks and Croats always lived there and lived there -- got along very well. Even after everything that has happened, there are many citizens of Croat background in the territory of Vitez municipality who have not changed a lot in their views -- at least those who I come across, those whom I had relationships with before the war, during the school years, and now, and those who had come from some other places as well. My personal view is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you to turn, if I may, to pages 44 and 45 of the Croatian version. Mr. Valenta makes the observations as follows, sir: If we bear in mind the truth that war solves nothing and that, to the contrary, everybody loses in a civil war, those articulate two ideas that -- with which you completely agree; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This is page 24 of the English version; I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true that nothing is resolved by war, that everybody loses in a war. But it is also true, unfortunately, that the war did take place there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Mr. Valenta goes on to say that -- let us force ourselves to think about that possibility, the possibility of a theoretical solution that he has earlier referred to, for the sake of the future of all three peoples. Let us think about it in order to protect hundreds of thousands of young people who would be killed in a stupid civil war. He also advocates ridding ourselves collectively of any Greater Croatian, Greater Serbian, or Greater Muslim egoism. You agree with all of those sentiments as well, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why didn't they then exist in many practical matters, on things that are not part of what the last sentence talks about? In terms of practical politics, this is my own question, but I'm a witness of the fact that the actions were different from what was written here, which is -- everything that is written here is fine, but the actual events went in a different direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And the last question I have on this subject concerns the conclusion, which we don't have, but we have an English translation of it, and basically, Mr. Valenta says, after expressing the ideas outlined in his book, that is why we must seek ways to create a happier life with independence and sovereignty for each nation. We must also help one another to accomplish that. The future will show us how and whether we shall succeed. He concludes -- and this is on page 49 of the version -- that the wish to divide Herceg-Bosna into a Muslim, a Serbian, and a Croatian region within the borders of the republic should be verified by a referendum. You have never heard Mr. Valenta at any time advocate the implementation of the ideas that he sets out in this book -- and some of which I've just read to you -- through the use of force, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here I have to take a step back. I keep saying that we would have been all very fortunate had everybody followed, in practical terms, what people were preaching. All this was a political war as much as it was a war for territories and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, Witness N.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It looks like the last topic that I had intended to cover with Witness N probably would not advance the ball very much, and I have no further questions, therefore, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think the transcript needs to be redacted from that inadvertent mention of the name of the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's nothing on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The video must be redacted, though. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness N, I will address you with the pseudonym which you got. I am Mr. Bozidar Kovacic, and alongside Mr. Mikulicic, I represent Mr. Cerkez. I only have a few clarifications for you, and the first one is you spent some time giving evidence on the Valenta book, both with the Prosecution and now with the Defence. From the copy of the book which I have, I see that the book was published, according to the regulations of that time, by a decision of the Ministry of Culture, Sport, of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So it's not any legal pamphlet or anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that the author of the book, Anto Valenta, is a historian who is an amateur, which is also put forth by the person who wrote the introduction to the book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that in Vitez, in October 1992, there were some meetings where people were looking for certain solutions, and you mentioned that one of the proposed solutions was for the military personnel to wear two badges, two different insignia. Do you also know of another attempt at compromise, that instead of HVO, a name HMVO be used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not recall that, but I did not attend any military meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In one of the meetings which was attended by both the civilians and the military, where Mr. Cilic was also present, did he propose such a thing? Does that bring any memories back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was only present at the first meeting, not at the second. I told you what was spoken during the first meeting. Then the meeting was interrupted, and the politicians of the Bosniak people and the SDA went in the field, so to speak, for consultations, to see what to do next.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could we then agree that in this meeting no solution was forced, or in these meetings -- perhaps that's how we should phrase it -- but, rather, common solution sought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some solutions sought in the first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But there were also attempts to find some solutions too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned the coordinating committee for the protection of Muslims. It was active between July and December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, until December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, did the local government in Vitez do anything to suppress or prevent the activities of this committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first we met in the municipal building. I think this was in July. Then we were forbidden to meet there, so we moved to the premises of the Merhamet organisation, which was in the fire station building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the HVO government in Vitez changed its position regarding the premises, that is, the offices which would be used but not with respect to its activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, the Bosniak representatives had been ousted from the local government and all activities took place in the Old Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the time when this committee was active and an attempt at having a parallel government, as you said, was there any administrating communication with Sarajevo? Did the administrative communication links operate at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am going to say yes, but I want to clarify it. I do not want to agree that the Bosniaks formed a parallel government. We never accepted that. One of the issues over which we had misunderstandings was this too, because Bosniaks held the position that the only legal power was the one which had been elected in the first open, free elections, and that its representatives were the only legal ones, and any other constructs we found illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: ... was the political position but the factual situation was different, and you just described a portion of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on, when the war was declared, then the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, through its decrees, it assumed the position of the assembly and then things followed as we know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You said, at one point during your evidence, that the identity of the Muslim people was always questioned as one of the constituent peoples. Isn't that true that the Bosnian Muslims were declared a nation in the 1960s, in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was in 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, but through the constitution it was legalised for the first time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But in that sense, the position of Muslims in the former Yugoslavia was somewhat different than the other -- that is, they were the only nation which had its religion as the basic identifying trait?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to another area. You said, and would you agree, that the 7th Muslim Brigade, which were -- where the Mujahedins also were, do you agree that even Muslims considered this unit to be an extremist one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This was not a generally shared opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, it wasn't. As a civilian, I do not even know that there was any military formation as Mujahedin. I never even attended any meetings, let alone know of any military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But in talking to friends and acquaintances --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there was the 7th Muslim Brigade. It was an armed component of the BH army, and what people said was that it did have religious rituals that it was conducting within the unit, but that was nothing special because in other ethnic groups similar things were also done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the barricade near Ahmici, below Ahmici, in October of 1992. Do you know that on those same days, the 19th and 20th of October, there was another barricade controlled by the Territorial Defence, that is, the BH army, further down the road near Bila, near the GP Bosna location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw this on local television. It was shown on local television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So there were two barricades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was shown on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness N, you pointed out that you were from Vitez and that you knew the situation in Vitez so far as you did, and is it true then, in 1992 and until 16 April, 1993, when the conflict broke out between these two ethnic groups, that throughout this period, in spite of the incidents in Vitez, in spite of the open conflict between these two ethnic groups in other -- even some of the surrounding municipalities, the politicians maintained dialogue, and they managed to keep things under a certain degree of control? Do you agree what that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can agree partially, but I need to add something with respect to the barricades. This was at the time when certain Bosniak and certain Croatian areas were protected by these barricades, so people should not be surprised by certain barricades being here or there. There was a barricade near Impregnacija, and then there was one towards Rijeka, one towards Kruscica. We're talking about the populated areas that were ours. That was the usual thing. It was also usual for people to pass through. People were just checking identities and things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But there was no widespread conflict in the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the 16th, no, there was not. There were attempts made for it not to ever take place. I'm sorry for banging on the desk. There were such attempts. On the 15th, a joint statement was issued that the talks would continue between the HDZ and SDA regarding the continuation of negotiations aimed at preventing the break-up of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness N, I only have a couple of questions for you in another area. You knew the Cerkez family before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Cerkez's parents, for a while after having moved to Vitez in the early 1960s, were subletting your apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my wife's apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you know them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The parents both worked at the post office, and Mario Cerkez worked in the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mario Cerkez from his childhood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When he first moved there, I was away studying, but then when I came back and when I married, then I met them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you knew him as a young man. Very well. Did you notice in the family, among any members, any prejudice against Bosnian Muslims or any ethnic groups who lived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is interesting to point out that until this time, no differences were ever noticed, not in conversation or in any kind of communication. It was only later. So in 1992 and later, all this came to the fore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that Mario Cerkez and his family were not an exception to this general rule?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. One more question. You mentioned that Cerkez was at this meeting attended by other persons on the Croatian side. You said that Valenta was there, and Skopljak was there, Santic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zvonko Cilic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in Mario Cerkez's presence. Did he attend there as a speaker? Was he there as a representative of the military component?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a representative of the military component.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, who was his military superior in Vitez at the level of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assumed that it was Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that Marijan Skopljak was the head of the chief of staff and Cerkez was his deputy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean Pero Skopljak's brother, that Marijan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The one that worked with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Pero Skopljak's brother. I only know that he wore a military uniform, but what he was in command of, I really don't know. I believe that at that time he was the chief of staff at the HVO. I know that his brother Pero was the head of police or the Ministry of the Interior in Vitez at the time. But he did wear a uniform all the time. He attended all kinds of meetings all the time, and I don't know what position he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to Marijan Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Cerkez was part of this staff that Marijan was the chief of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oftentimes when I say something, I don't know the internal structure of this organisation, and I told the gentlemen that we shouldn't go into these details because I just don't know them. I was not present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just one more question in connection with this meeting. You said that Zvonko Cilic was also present there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you perhaps tell us in what position he attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in the position of a local journalist, because that is what he did at the time. He had a joint television station at the time, so there were joint statements being issued. At the time, this was his --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. This concludes my questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have some questions in re-examination. I don't know whether the Court wants me to deal with them. It will take five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Deal with them now if you can, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I do that, on the revelation of a name that is protected -- I think that's happened now several times in the last few days -- I don't know if the Chamber wanted to say anything to the press who are, of course, represented in the room here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The matter has been redacted from the video. I'm sure the press know what the rules are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness N, you were asked about uniforms being worn by non-military personnel. Just yes or no: Do you have any personal experience of that happening at the time, a military uniform being worn by non-military personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the phenomenon of the times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What sort of people were doing it, people of all ages, or particular ages? Just give us the picture, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uniforms were mostly worn by able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about your job -- don't say anything that will reveal what your job was -- and Bosniaks losing their positions of authority. Two points arising from that. Can you explain in a sentence, without revealing what your job was, why you didn't leave your job until the outbreak on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked in the Sintevit factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, don't -- let me deal with it this way: Did you hold a specialist job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to stop you straightaway. I'm going to move on. Before the October 1992 meeting, so far as you were concerned, had there been an order or similar issued by Rajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bozo Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that an order was issued, when he became Minister, regarding the uniting of the armed components of the BH army and the HVO, and in my first statement, I said that I did not recollect the date but there was such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Cerkez, you've been asked some questions about him and about his role at that meeting where you saw him. What was his role at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that meeting, the role of Mr. Cerkez was a purely military role.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His military role being?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Commander of a brigade, I think he was, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How was Valenta treated, if you saw this, by other HVO officers and senior people? How was he treated or regarded by them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally believe that he was higher up in the hierarchy. Not in the military, but he was looked upon as a senior official in the HDZ hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reference in his book to "Greater Croatia egoism," does that ever come about, in your judgement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we'll be helped by that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The raising of the question of partitioning of ethnic groups dealt with in this book, did that have any effect either on you or, to your knowledge, any other Bosniaks who read the book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people who read the book or who were superficially informed about its contents did not have positive comments to make about such ideas and thoughts that it contained.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked a question by Judge Bennouna about ethnic cooperation. You gave a fairly substantial answer, at the end of which you said your personal view, but you were dealing with the same topic. Was there anything on the cooperation and coexistence of the ethnic groups that you wanted to say at that stage that you haven't since dealt with in your other answers? Can you remember if there's anything else you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In those days?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, before the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war. I said that even under those circumstances, neighbours helped one another as much as they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 7th Muslim Brigade, you've spoken of its religious ceremonies. Can you just give us an example of them, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't talking about religious ceremonies. I just said that they recognised their faith. They practised their faith. That, according to regulations, they prayed to God at the set times. I was never amongst them to see this, to check whether they prayed five times a day or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was there any aspect of religious observance that was extremist or that was imported from outside Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally believe that the word "God" -- because the word "God" could not be mentioned in public, because it was well known that Muslims or Bosniaks of Islamic faith pray in Arabic, the mention of the word "God" was not accepted in these parts. So this too had certain connotations when the word "God" or "Allah" was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But was any part of their ritual or observance, so far as you knew, imported specifically from some other country, Mujahedin or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as religious rites are concerned, they cannot be imported, because a Bosniak of Islamic faith who is a strict believer is obliged to pray to God five times a day -- let me not enumerate those occasions -- and it is in that context that I view the behaviour of the members of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last question, for clarification: You were asked, on Mr. Cerkez's behalf, questions that led to your saying all people were getting on, as it were, before the war, and that what happened thereafter happened to a lot of people, or was seen to happen to a lot of people, in their change of attitude. You were asked if Cerkez was an exception to this rule, and the answer you gave was no. I just want to know whether you're saying he behaved in the same way as other people, so far as change of attitude was concerned, or if he behaved in any different way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Cerkez behaved in accordance with the positions advocated by Herceg-Bosna. I'm making no distinction between political and military. That is my personal view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness N, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should like to thank Your Honours for giving me this opportunity to speak before you. I have sought to present the truth as I saw it, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll sit again at 2.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.12 p.m. 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask at this time for a private session for the purpose of bringing before the Court an application on measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Before that's done, it should be noted that Mr. Cerkez is back in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may just add, Your Honour, related to the order which facilitated his temporary release, everything was fully respected, only that at this moment, at least, I'm not aware that the paper from the Croatian authorities, the report which you ordered, has come. Probably it's on the way. But I will inquire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 4.16 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 21st day of September, 1999 at 11.30 a.m. 24 25
